questions.question: Explain why the VOC decided to set up a station at the Cape in 1652.
questions.expected_answer: The VOC (founded 1602) traded spices between Asia and Europe for profit; the voyage to Batavia took six months or more, fresh food ran out and many sailors died of scurvy (lack of vitamin C). The Company needed a halfway station for fresh water, vegetables, fruit and meat, to treat the sick and repair ships. The 1647 wreck of the Nieuwe Haarlem and the 1649 Remonstrantie showed the Cape had fertile soil, good water and Khoikhoi willing to trade cattle; a fort would also protect the route from rivals.

questions.question: Describe the first years of the station under Jan van Riebeeck.
questions.expected_answer: Van Riebeeck arrived on 6 April 1652 with three ships (Drommedaris, Reijger, Goede Hoop); built an earth and wood fort (later the stone Castle of Good Hope, 1666-1679) and the Company's Garden; the first winter brought illness, food shortages and damaged gardens; Khoikhoi would not sell as many cattle as wanted; employees were not meant to settle permanently until 1657.

questions.question: How did the VOC station affect the Khoikhoi in its first years?
questions.expected_answer: Trade became unequal and cattle were sometimes taken by force; in 1657 Khoikhoi grazing land along the Liesbeek River was given to free burghers and later marked by a bitter almond hedge; the Khoikhoi, led by Doman, resisted in the First Khoikhoi-Dutch War (1659-1660); at the peace talks they protested that the land was theirs and were told it had been lost in war - the start of dispossession. Krotoa served as interpreter between the two worlds.
